claims.text: A query that contains the shard key can be sent to exactly one shard; a query without it cannot rule out any shard, so it must ask all of them and merge the answers (scatter-gather).
claims.source_hint: content/glossary.yaml scatter-gather, shard-key; ShardedOrders.cs @ stage-3 lines 11-14, 28-32

claims.text: shard-split.sh lines 19-30 create donhang_shard_0/1, load shard-schema.sql into each, and COPY the orders with customer_id % 2 = shard out of donhang_perf into that shard; psql_in_db (lines 10-12) runs psql in the db container that scripts/up.sh starts, so both databases are on one server.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-3 scripts/backend/shard-split.sh lines 10-30; db/sharding/shard-schema.sql; scripts/up.sh

claims.text: A PostgreSQL connection reaches one database, so a plain query run on donhang_shard_N cannot read donhang_perf's tables; the script moves the rows with COPY ... TO STDOUT (rows written to the command's output) piped into COPY ... FROM STDIN (rows read from its input into the table).
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 22.1 Managing Databases, Overview; SQL command COPY

claims.text: shard-split.sh builds donhang_perf first if it does not exist (perf-db.sh --if-missing, line 8), and runs the sharded-orders sample on the host with dotnet run (line 36), so it needs the .NET SDK on the machine; a first run that must build donhang_perf takes longer.

Output @ stage-3: shard_0 20000, shard_1 180000 orders; customer 7 on shard 1 (orders 199986, 199886, 199786); 30 newest = orders 199971-200000, 10 from shard 0 and 20 from shard 1; with 15 from each, 5 of 30 are not among the newest.
donhang_perf: 20 customers, 200,000 orders, customer 1 placed 81%, customers 2-20 1% each; so odd ids (shard 1) hold 162,000 + 9 x 2,000 = 180,000 orders (9 in 10), even ids 20,000.
ShardFor returns customerId % shards.Count, and LatestForCustomerAsync queries only that shard (WHERE customer_id = @customer_id ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT @count); 7 % 2 = 1.
LatestOnShardAsync runs SELECT ... ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT @count on one shard, so each shard returns its own newest count orders.

For the N newest overall, each shard must return N rows: the true N newest may all be on one shard, so a shard returning fewer can omit some, and the merge cannot detect it. Demo: 15+15 misses 5 of 30.
claims.source_hint: ShardedOrders.cs comment lines 30-31; ShardedOrdersDemo.cs; shard-split.txt line 11

claims.text: Calling an async method returns its Task without waiting for it to finish; collecting one Task per shard and then awaiting Task.WhenAll lets the shard queries be in progress at the same time.
claims.source_hint: .NET 10 docs: Asynchronous programming with async and await (start tasks, then await Task.WhenAll); Task.WhenAll API reference

claims.text: Task.WhenAll returns a task that completes when all supplied tasks have completed; if any supplied task faults, the returned task is faulted and awaiting it throws.
Merge flattens the per-shard lists (SelectMany), sorts by PlacedAt descending then Id descending (ThenByDescending breaks ties between equal PlacedAt, so the order is fixed), and takes count (Take).
claims.source_hint: ShardedOrders.cs @ stage-3 lines 46-52; .NET 10 API reference: Enumerable.SelectMany, OrderByDescending, ThenByDescending, Take

claims.text: A scatter-gather result is ready only when the slowest shard answers, and needs every shard: a down shard means an error or a result silently missing that shard's rows.
claims.source_hint: Follows from waiting on all shards (Task.WhenAll); ShardedOrders.cs comment line 32; outline item 5

claims.text: When a query without the shard key runs often: if most reads lack the key, the key is wrong; if most use it and a few frequent ones do not, serve those from a read model in its own database, filled by messages from every shard, so eventually consistent.
claims.source_hint: Condition stated (frequent queries without the shard key); outline item 5; prereq design.l3.read-model; claim 15 (one transaction reaches one database)

claims.text: An ordinary transaction runs on one connection, and a PostgreSQL connection reaches one database; rows on two shards change in two transactions, one of which can commit while the other fails.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 22.1 Managing Databases, Overview; SQL command BEGIN; prereq backend.l3.sharding

claims.text: Keeping changes on two shards consistent needs the tools for a change across services, such as a saga with compensating actions.
Two-phase commit could make two shards commit together, but a prepared transaction keeps holding its locks until the coordinator commits or rolls it back.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: SQL command PREPARE TRANSACTION (Notes); related backend.l3.two-phase-commit

claims.text: ANALYZE collects statistics about the contents of a table, which the query planner uses to choose query plans.
